Google Business Profile ranking tricks for a local business, and the ones that get you suspended

Categories, services, products, photos, posts, questions and a steady flow of real reviews. Then the black-hat moves people try, from keyword-stuffed names to review swaps, and why they end in suspension or worse.
Google says local ranking comes down to relevance, distance and prominence, and that nobody can pay for a better spot. The tricks that work feed relevance and prominence.
Pick the right primary category, fill in services and products, post photos and updates, answer questions, and ask every client for a review.
Keyword-stuffed names, fake listings, bought reviews and review swaps break Google’s rules. Bought and fake reviews also break the FTC’s 2024 rule.
For a local business, the Google Business Profile is often the first thing a new client sees. It is the card in the map. It shows up before your website does.

Google says plainly how that map is ranked. [Three things](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en): **relevance** (how well your profile matches the search), **distance** (how far you are from the searcher) and **prominence** (how well-known you are, including links and reviews). It also says there is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking. You cannot move your shop closer. So every trick below works on relevance and prominence.
Categories: the setting that matters most

Your primary category tells Google what you are. Pick the most specific one that fits your core business. “Kitchen remodeler” beats “contractor” if that is what you do. Google's [profile guidelines](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177?hl=en) say to use as few categories as possible, and never to use a category just as a keyword.

How much does it matter? Google does not publish weights. In Whitespark's [Local Search Ranking Factors survey](https://whitespark.ca/local-search-ranking-factors), local search experts ranked the primary category the top factor for the map results. That is expert opinion, not a Google statement, but it lines up with what Google says about relevance.

These are the most skipped fields, and they are free relevance. [Services](https://support.google.com/business/answer/9455399?hl=en) let you list exactly what you do, with a description and a price if you want. [Products](https://support.google.com/business/answer/9124203?hl=en) let you show items or packages with a photo each.

Name each service the way clients search for it: “water heater replacement,” not “Plumbing Solutions Package B.” A product does not have to be a physical thing. A dentist can list “teeth whitening” with a photo and a price range. Keep it honest. Google's guidelines say a product policy violation can get your whole catalog removed.
Photos and posts: a steady cadence

Google tells owners to add [photos and videos](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en) that show what they offer, and to keep hours and details current. It does not say how often. “Post a photo every week or you drop” is folklore. The useful version: add real photos regularly, so the profile always looks open and alive.
Shoot the outside of the building, so people recognize it. Then the team, the work and finished jobs. No stock photos: they say nothing about you.

Profiles can also publish [posts](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7662907?hl=en): updates, offers and events, shown on Search and Maps. Offers can sit near the top of the profile. Post the same things you post on social media: a finished job, this month's offer, an event. It is one more reason for a searcher to pick you.

The description is where you say who you serve and what you do, in your own words. BrightLocal's guide puts the limit at [750 characters, with no links](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/google-business-profile-description/), and notes that only the start shows before “More.” So say the most important thing first: what you do, and where.

Questions have changed. In late 2025 Google [replaced the public Q&A section in Maps](https://ppc.land/google-quietly-kills-q-a-for-an-ai-button-most-wont-use/) with an “Ask” button that gives AI answers. The answers draw on what the business has provided and on reviews. Owners can still answer questions from the profile, and those answers feed the AI. So the trick now is simple: keep every detail complete and true, because that is what Google's answers are built from.

Google says [more reviews and positive ratings can help](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en) local ranking. Some local SEO experts believe how recent your reviews are now counts more, too. Whitespark calls review recency [one of its top five factors](https://whitespark.beehiiv.com/p/the-most-underrated-local-ranking-factor-in-2025-e544). That is their view, not Google's.

The honest trick is a habit: ask every client, every time, right after the job. Google gives you a [review link and a QR code](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122) for exactly this. Put it in the thank-you email, on the receipt, on the counter.

**Every** client is the important word. Google's [contribution policy](https://support.google.com/contributionpolicy/answer/7400114?hl=en) bans selectively asking only happy clients for reviews, and bans discouraging negative ones. That is called review gating. It also bans incentives: no discounts, gifts or payment for a review. And it bans reviews from staff or anyone with a conflict of interest.

Then reply to reviews, good and bad. Google says replies show clients that [their feedback matters](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122). A calm reply to a bad review is read by every future client who sees it.

NAP means name, address and phone number. Keep them exactly the same on your profile, your website, Facebook, Yelp and every directory that lists you. Google says [complete and accurate information](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en) helps you show up. How much matching directory listings, called citations, help ranking is an industry belief, not something Google publishes. BrightLocal warns that [inconsistent details](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/local-seo/what-is-nap/) can hurt your local presence and your clients' trust. Either way, a wrong phone number on a directory loses you the call.
The black-hat tricks, and why they get suspended

**Keyword-stuffed business names.** Renaming “Smith Plumbing” to “Smith Plumbing Emergency Plumber Dallas 24/7.” People try it because it can work for a while: experts in the same [Whitespark survey](https://whitespark.ca/local-search-ranking-factors) ranked keywords in the business name near the top. But Google's [guidelines](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177?hl=en) say your name must match your real-world name, and that adding extra words can get the profile suspended. Competitors can report it through Google's [complaint form](https://searchengineland.com/google-opens-complaint-form-to-crack-down-on-fake-info-in-maps-313173), and a person reviews it.

**Fake listings and virtual offices.** Extra profiles at a mailbox, a coworking desk or a friend's address, to show up in more towns. Google's guidelines require a real-world location, ban P.O. boxes and remote mailboxes, and allow one profile per business per location. A service-area business should hide its address and set a service area instead. Fake listings get removed, and Google can suspend access to your profiles.

**Buying reviews, or writing your own.** This is where the rules become the law. The FTC's [rule on fake reviews](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/08/federal-trade-commission-announces-final-rule-banning-fake-reviews-testimonials), in force since October 2024, bans buying, selling or writing fake reviews, including AI-written ones. It bans paying for reviews on the condition that they are positive, and undisclosed reviews from owners, managers and staff. Law firms reported penalties of [up to $51,744 per violation](https://dwt.com/insights/2024/08/ftc-finalizes-rule-banning-fake-consumer-reviews).

**Review swaps.** “I review your shop, you review mine.” Google's policy bans reviews with a conflict of interest, including personal and professional ties, and flags unusual patterns of reviews. A swap is a conflict of interest.
**Burying bad reviews.** Threatening a client to take a review down is review suppression, and the FTC rule bans that too. Google's own rule also bars discouraging negative reviews.

What Google does about it: it removes fake and incentivized reviews. When it catches a pattern, it can show a [consumer alert](https://support.google.com/contributionpolicy/answer/15178562?hl=en) on your profile saying suspicious reviews were removed, and stop new reviews for a while. A warning label on your own listing is the opposite of growth.

Can I pay Google for a better map ranking?
No. Google says there is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking. Local ranking comes from relevance, distance and prominence.
Can I offer a discount for a Google review?
No. Google’s policy bans incentives for reviews, including discounts, gifts and payment, and removes reviews posted because of one.
Is it OK to only ask happy clients for reviews?
No. Google bans selectively asking for positive reviews, which is called review gating. Ask every client.
Can keywords in my business name get my profile suspended?
Yes. Google’s guidelines say your name must match your real-world name, and that extra words in it can lead to suspension.
